questions.question_text:
Many recreational drugs are associated with a degree of dependence, either physiological or psychological. Which of the following
substances has the lowest risk of dependence?
questions.explanation:
LSD has the lowest risk of dependence of the drugs listed. “Abuse of LSD is rather di�cult; the drug produces such an absurd high that daily
ingestion is almost impossible. Thus LSD use does not lead to physical dependence. However, the tolerance as mentioned disappears after a
few days of abstinence without producing craving. So, LSD dependence is typically psychological and not physical [Gable, 1993; Bogenschutz
et al. 2015]”. The other substances mentioned have, to a greater or lesser extent, a signi�cant risk of psychological dependence. Ref: Excerpt
from Das S, et al. Lysergic acid diethylamide: a drug of 'use’?. Therapeutic advances in psychopharmacology. 2016 Jun;6(3):214-28.

questions.question_text: Staccato speech is most commonly associated with;
questions.explanation:
Staccato speech is when an individual speaks in fragments of sentences that are punctuated by pauses, which interrupt sentence, to the
point of destroying the �ow of speech. Such speech is abrupt, broken, and usually quite hard to follow. It is associated with cerebellar
disease. Ref: Lechtenberg R, Gilman S. Speech disorders in cerebellar disease. Annals of Neurology. 1978 Apr;3(4):285-90.

Mr Harry Clyde is a 45-year-old man with a long history of alcohol misuse. His family have brought him to his local A&E as they were
concerned about him. He has subsequently been diagnosed with Korsako� Syndrome. Which of the following is the most common
symptom of this disorder?
questions.explanation:
Anterograde amnesia and a variable degree of retrograde amnesia are the most common symptoms of Korsako�’s syndrome.
Confabulation can occur as a consequence but is not seen in all cases. Ref: Lishman’s Organic Psychiatry

questions.question_text:
Sarah Hughes is a 25-year-old woman with a 2-hour-old newborn who is noted to be very irritable, restless, tremulous and inconsolably
crying. Which of the following substances did her mother most likely use during pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Heroin withdrawal tends to be seen within 24 hours of birth, as with other short acting opioids. Signs and symptoms include excessive
crying, tremors, increased muscle tone and re�exes. Similar withdrawal presentations are seen with other drugs, although this is less
frequent with alcohol and cannabis.

questions.question_text:
Buprenorphine is seen as a useful medication for opioid substitution as it has signi�cantly di�erent properties to methadone. In which of
the following ways is buprenorphine di�erent to methadone?

options.text: It has no risk of respiratory depression
More marked withdrawals if abruptly stopped
Buprenorphine can be given orally or intravenously

correct_answer.text: Buprenorphine can be given orally or intravenously

questions.explanation:
There are combined buprenorphine and naloxone preparations available for oral and intravenous administration although their e�cacy is
still unclear. Buprenorphine can cause respiratory depression in high doses or in associations with other psychotropics. It and methadone
are generally given orally. Methadone has higher treatment retention and has more severe withdrawals if abruptly stopped. Buprenorphine
has a ceiling e�ect with good safety pro�le. Methadone does not have ceiling e�ect and useful in patients dependent on high doses of
opioids.

questions.question_text:
Mr Howard Hughes is a 43-year-old man who has repeatedly attended his GP surgery and local A&E with concerns that something is
blocking his throat. He has had numerous negative investigations, including direct visualisation of his pharynx, which can temporarily
reassure him. Nevertheless, he continues to present himself. When asked, he describes a sense of something in his throat and is clearly very
anxious. This is most likely to be
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to be hypochondriasis as the patient has an overvalued idea about a particular diagnosis. In somatisation disorder,
patients describe numerous and often changeable physical symptoms. Patients experiencing psychotic symptoms would generally not be
reassured, even temporarily, by negative investigation �ndings. Note that DSM-5 prefers the term Somatic Symptom Disorder for the same
presentation.

questions.question_text:
Post-natal depression can lead to signi�cant distress in new mothers and impair their ability to bond with and care for their newborn
children. What percentage of new mothers su�ers from postnatal depression?
questions.explanation:
It is thought that 10-15% of new mothers experience post-natal depression, with rates reducing to <10% after 12 weeks postpartum. Ref:
Leahy-Warren et al., Arch Psychiatr Nurs. 2011 Jun;25(3):174-84

questions.question_text:
Inpatient suicide rates in the UK have reduced signi�cantly since 2000. Which of the following is thought to have contributing most to this
decrease?

options.text: Use of formal risk assessment tools

questions.explanation:
In the UK, hanging was the reported method in 77% of inpatient suicides between 1999 and 2007. The most common ligature points were
doors, hooks or handles, windows, belts, and sheets or towels. Removal of ligature points had a signi�cant impact on the rate of inpatient
suicides, though the use of shoelaces, doors, and windows increased over time. Ref; Bowers, L.; Dack, C.; Gul, N.; Thomas, B.; James, K.
(2011) Learning from prevented suicide in psychiatric inpatient care: An analysis of data from the National Patient Safety Agency.
International Journal of Nursing Studies 48 (12) 1459-1465

questions.question_text:
People with schizophrenia can have certain cognitive impairments that are present when they are not experiencing an episode of psychosis.
Which of the following is most common?
questions.explanation: The most common cognitive impairments in schizophrenia are those around executive functioning and working memory.

questions.question_text:
Mr Charlie Simms is a 26-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with schizophrenia. Once he has recovered he is keen to know
more about his prognosis and what factors might have an impact on it. Which of the following factors is most likely to support a favourable
prognosis?
questions.explanation:
A family history of a�ective disorder is associated with a positive prognosis, as is having a�ective symptoms during episodes of illness. Acute
onset, short duration of untreated symptoms, older age of onset, good premorbid functioning, being in a stable relationship and having a
good support system are all positive prognostic factors in schizophrenia.

questions.question_text:
Puerperal psychosis is a psychotic illness that tends to occur shortly after a woman gives birth. Which of the following is the most common
presentation?
questions.explanation:
Prominent a�ective symptoms and unusual behaviour are the most common presenting symptoms in puerperal psychosis. This is often
associated with profound anxiety and this can be associated with persecutory ideation. Many patients later satisfy the criteria for psychotic
bipolar disorder.

questions.question_text:
Mr Edward Hughes is a 23-year-old man with autism spectrum disorder and moderate intellectual impairment. He lives in a placement and
has been demonstrating aggressive behaviour over the last several months. Attempts to identify the cause of his distress or address his
behaviour via non-pharmacological methods have been fruitless. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for him?
questions.explanation:
Risperidone and Aripiprazole have the greatest evidence base for the pharmacological management of aggression in ASD. Other second-
and �rst-generation antipsychotics, antiepileptic medications, lithium, naltrexone and N-acetylcysteine have also been used although with
less evidence being available for these agents.

questions.question_text:
Mr Neil Peterson is a 36-year-old man who is currently experiencing a moderate depressive episode. He is struggling to motivate himself to
engage with his usual activities and is due to be assessed for behavioural activation therapy. Which of the following will this include?
questions.explanation:
Assessment for behavioural activation therapy includes identi�cation of TRAP (Trigger, Response, Avoidance Pattern) with the avoidance
including direct avoidance, rumination and use of alcohol, drugs and other maladaptive coping strategies. The aim is to replace this with
TRAC (Trigger, Response, Alternate Coping response). Ref: Weinstock LM, Munroe MK, Miller IW. Behavioral activation for the treatment of
atypical depression: a pilot open trial. Behavior modi�cation. 2011 Jul;35(4):403-24.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Susan Matthews is a 42-year-old woman with a previous diagnosis of bipolar a�ective disorder. She has been well without medication
for three years but has now presented with a clear-cut episode of depression. Which of the following would be most appropriate to treat
her?
questions.explanation:
NICE recommends that individuals with a diagnosis of bipolar depression, who are not currently receiving medication, should be prescribed
either Olanzapine and Fluoxetine in combo or Quetiapine by itself as �rst line treatment. Patients can choose to have Olanzapine without
Fluoxetine if desired (but not the antidepressant alone). Lamotrigine can also be o�ered if the above therapies are ine�ective or the patient
expresses a preference for it. Ref:

questions.question_text:
ECT is a highly e�ective intervention in those with severe episodes of depression, which are treatment resistant or associated with risk to
life. Which of the following is true about ECT?

options.text: Seizures on EEG last longer than the physical seizure
A history of Ischemic heart disease is an absolute contraindication for ECT
ECT can only be delivered for inpatients
An ECT-induced seizure lasting longer than 2 minutes should be pharmacologically aborted
Antidepressants should be discontinued while ECT is delivered.

correct_answer.text: Seizures on EEG last longer than the physical seizure

questions.explanation:
It is common for seizure activity on the EEG to continue for longer than the physical movements, particularly as patients receiving ECT will
have also have been administered a muscle relaxant. Ref: Fink M, Abrams R. EEG monitoring in ECT: a guide to treatment e�cacy. Psychiatric
Times, May. 1998 May 1;15(5).

questions.question_text:
Tina Keyes is a 2-year-old girl who was born with a cleft palate, which is in the process of being surgically repaired. She demonstrated
evidence of development delay during her �rst year and it is now thought that she will likely have a degree of intellectual disability. Which of
the following medications taken during pregnancy is most likely to have contributed to these problems?
questions.explanation:
Sodium valproate should not be prescribed to women of childbearing age unless other therapies are ine�ective or inappropriate. If taken
throughout pregnancy, about 10% of infants will have a congenital malformation and 40% will have a degree of developmental delay and
intellectual impairment. Sertraline and other SSRIs are associated with a small increase in the risk of congenital malformations. Lithium was
associated with an increase in the risk of congenital malformations, particularly Ebstein's anomaly. Benzodiazepines were considered to be
associated with cleft lip and palate, but recent studies indicate that the risk is much lower than what was thought before. Antipsychotics,
with the exception of risperidone, which shows a small increase in the risk of cardiac defects, are not associated with congenital
abnormalities or developmental problems.

questions.question_text:
Mr Vincent Payes is a 38-year-old man with a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia. He has had a recent relapse, which has been successfully
treated with Olanzapine, but he reports that it makes him rather sedated during the day, including when he is driving. It appears likely that it
is impairing his ability to drive. Which of the following should be done?

options.text: Report the patient's inability to drive to the DVLA directly
Advise the patient to stop driving and report to the DVLA themselves
Advise the patient to omit the Olanzapine if they have to drive the next day
Advise the patient to continue to drive but be cautious

correct_answer.text: Advise the patient to stop driving and report to the DVLA themselves

questions.explanation:
The patient needs to stop driving if their medication may be impairing their ability to do so safely. It is usually appropriate to advise the
patient to stop driving and inform the DVLA. It may then be appropriate to modify their prescription so they are not so sedated during the
day, provided this does not compromise their mental wellbeing. If a patient will not inform the DVLA himself or herself, then it is appropriate
to contact them directly. The patient's con�dentiality can be breached for this purpose.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Yanica Presley is a 32-year-old woman with a previous diagnosis of bipolar a�ective disorder and has had several previous episodes of
mania requiring admission. She has responded well to Lithium and has had no relapses since it was started 3 years ago. She is currently 36
weeks pregnant and has been taking Lithium 600mg throughout her pregnancy. She is currently well in her mood and is not planning on
breastfeeding. Which of the following would be the most appropriate action?

options.text: Do nothing and review after 1 week after delivery
Reduce dose to 400 mg, then repeat blood levels after 1 week
Continue lithium and check levels weekly until delivery and for 2 weeks after

correct_answer.text: Continue lithium and check levels weekly until delivery and for 2 weeks after

questions.explanation:
Lithium can be continued throughout pregnancy provided that adequate monitoring is provided. This is usually 4 weekly until 34 weeks and
then weekly until 2 weeks post-partum, with doses being modi�ed as appropriate. An increase in dose is often required earlier in the
pregnancy with this reversing to an extent in late pregnancy. Lithium can be omitted for 24-48 prior to labour to reduce e�ects on the
newborn but this must be balanced against the risk of relapse in high risk women. Women at high risk of relapse in the post-partum must
not be left without e�ective treatment.

questions.question_text:
Parkinsonism describes a collection of physical symptoms, which are usually caused by a lack of active dopamine in certain areas of the
thalamus. It can occur as a consequence of antipsychotic medication. Which of the following is the Parkinsonian symptom most likely to be
seen in association with antipsychotic use?
questions.explanation:
Rigidity and bradykinesia are seen more commonly in individuals with drug-induced Parkinsonism than those with Parkinson's disease,
where pill-rolling tremor is more common. Drug-induced Parkinsonism tends to be bilateral initially.

questions.question_text:
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a new physical intervention in psychiatry that is increasingly being used outside of research settings. Which
of the following is an indication for DBS?
questions.explanation:
DBS is indicated in Parkinson's disease, which is refractory to or complicated by medical therapy. It can also be used in movement disorders
(dystonia or tremors), depression, OCD, Tourette's Syndrome, epilepsy, cluster headache and chronic pain.

questions.question_text:
Abdominal pain is a common presenting symptom amongst children seen in paediatric practice. Which of the following is true regarding
abdominal pain in children?

options.text: Abdominal pain is a common symptom of anxiety in children
Abdominal pain is usually associated with a persistent disturbance in appetite
Abdominal pain related to anxiety in children is usually very well localised to one spot
Abdominal pain in children usually responds readily to medical interventions
Abdominal pain is usually associated with clear bowel symptoms

correct_answer.text: Abdominal pain is a common symptom of anxiety in children

questions.explanation:
Abdominal pain in children, whilst it can occasionally be due to signi�cant organic pathology, is usually ill de�ned and without clearly
associated physical symptoms. It is commonly associated with anxiety and worry. Ref; Cunningham NR, et al. Importance of addressing
anxiety in youth with functional abdominal pain: suggested guidelines for physicians. Journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition.
2013 May;56(5):469.

questions.question_text:
Reading di�culties are relatively common and a�ected children and adults may need certain adaptations to engage with education and
work. What is the male: female ratio of reading di�culties?
questions.explanation:
If reading di�culties are de�ned as 2 standard deviations below mean, then the male: female ratio is 2:1. If 3 standard deviations are used,
this increases to 4:1 due to the greater variance in male reading ability. Ref: Arnett AB, et al. Explaining the sex di�erence in dyslexia. Journal
of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 2017 Jun;58(6):719-27.

questions.question_text:
Anorexia nervosa most commonly a�ects females and is characterised by body image distortion and behaviours focused upon losing
weight, most commonly in terms of dietary restriction but also excessive exercise and purging. When is it most likely to present?
questions.explanation: The average age of onset of anorexia nervosa is 16-17 years.

questions.question_text:
Sam Allen is a 10-year-old boy who has been referred to their local CAMHS clinic after it was noted that they were speaking at home but not
at school. They are subsequently diagnosed with selective mutism. Which of the following is true regarding selective mutism?

options.text: Usually not associated with other mental disorder
It tends to entirely resolve over several months

questions.explanation:
Selective mutism is relatively rare, occurring in about 0.71% of children. It is highly associated with other anxiety disorders, particularly social
phobia. It may be more common in girls than boys and tends to present between the ages of 3-6 years, when a child enters nursery or
primary school. Children who recover tend to have ongoing social and talking di�culties.

questions.question_text:
Autism spectrum disorders are characterised by impairments in social interactions and communication and restricted and repetitive
interests. They can also be associated with language delay and intellectual impairment. Which of the following is the greatest risk factor for
the development of an autism spectrum disorder?
questions.explanation:
A low 5-minute APGAR score is associated with later ASD. Other perinatal risk factors for ASD are: abnormal presentation, umbilical-cord
complications, foetal distress, birth injury or trauma, multiple birth, maternal hemorrhage, summer birth, low birth weight, small for
gestational age, congenital malformation, feeding di�culties, meconium aspiration, neonatal anemia, ABO or Rh incompatibility, and
hyperbilirubinemia. Overalll, genetic factors are the greatest known risk factors for ASD. Ref; Modabbernia A, Sandin S, Gross R, Leonard H,
Gissler M, Parner ET, Francis R, Carter K, Bresnahan M, Schendel D, Hornig M. Apgar score and risk of autism. European journal of
epidemiology. 2018 Oct 5:1-0.

questions.question_text:
Conduct disorder is a disorder seen in adolescents characterised by repeatedly de�ant and transgressing behaviour, often with aggression,
rule breaking and other criminal behaviour. Which of the following is the most appropriate �rst line intervention?
questions.explanation:
Parental psychoeducation and training is most e�ective in conduct disorder so they can e�ectively establish and maintain boundaries with
the child and enable positive behavioural strategies to be enacted. Achieving behavioural change without clear boundaries and routines is
very challenging.

questions.question_text:
James Borden is a 16-year boy who has been experiencing a moderate depressive episode for the last 6 months. He has received a course of
CBT without signi�cant e�ect on his symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for his management?
questions.explanation:
If a child with depression has had an adequate course of CBT without success it is most appropriate to start Fluoxetine as the next step.
Fluoxetine is recommended in children, as it is less likely than other antidepressants to cause an increase in suicidal ideation.

questions.question_text:
Richard Arbuthnot is an 8-year-old boy who has been referred to the local CAMHS clinic. He is struggling at school due to an inability to sit
still or concentrate on any academic tasks. He has also been noted to make a repeated throat clearing noise and twist his head sideways.
Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for him?
questions.explanation:
This patient is presenting with symptoms consistent with both ADHD and Tourette's syndrome. In these cases, provided the ADHD is not
very disabling and Tourette's relatively mild, it is most reasonable to trial Clonidine or guanfacine in the �rst instance. Methylphenidate
would be likely to worsen his vocal and motor tics.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with respect to Tourette's disorder?

options.text: Diagnosis involves having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months
The treatment of choice is with antipsychotics
It is rare for it to co-exist with ASD
It can be diagnosed if symptoms start at any age.
Diagnosis involves having both motor and vocal tics for 6 months

correct_answer.text: Diagnosis involves having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months

questions.explanation:
Tourette's Syndrome requires the presence of both motor and vocal tics for at least 12 months. They need not occur at the same time but
some tics should be evident throughout this time period. Alpha-2-adrenergic agonists, such as clonidine, are often used �rst line.

questions.question_text:
Some studies have reported a strong correlation between adverse events to SSRIs and their therapeutic e�cacy. This has led to the
suggestion that the improvement seen in patients allocated to active drug treatment could have been exaggerated as study participants
became aware of allocation by experiencing adverse events. To investigate further whether adverse events mediated the relationship
between treatment and e�cacy, a mediation framework was used by Barth et al. (2016). The result of this analysis is given in the graph.
Which of the following conditions must be met in order to establish a mediation e�ect?

options.text: The predictor must relate to the outcome only when controlled for the mediator
The relationship between predictor and outcome must be reduced when controlled for the mediator
The suspected mediator must not be related to the outcome
Predictor must not be related to the suspected mediator
Predictor must not be related to the outcome

correct_answer.text: The relationship between predictor and outcome must be reduced when controlled for the mediator

questions.explanation:
According to Barron & Kenny's mediation model approach mediation e�ect is said to be present when four conditions are met: 1. The
predictor (i.e. treatment) must be signi�cantly related to the outcome (i.e. response). This is shown as pathway c in the graph; 2. The
predictor must also be signi�cantly related to the potential mediator (adverse events). This is shown as pathway a in the graph; 3. The
mediator must be signi�cantly related to the outcome when the e�ect of the predictor on the outcome is controlled for; This is shown as
pathway b in the graph 4. The relationship between predictor and outcome must be reduced when controlling for the mediator (i.e. pathway
c' having e�ect lower than the pathway c).

became aware of allocation by experiencing adverse events. To investigate further whether adverse events mediated the relationship

correct_answer.text: Adverse e�ects are proportional to the response

questions.explanation:
Treatment with an SSRI appears to be signi�cantly associated with both response (b = 0.499, SE = 0.071, P<0.001) and with higher rates of

=70.036, SE = 0.041, P= 0.384). The direct relationship between SSRI treatment and treatment response under control of adverse events
(pathway c') is statistically signi�cant (b = 0.524, SE = 0.077, P<0.001). As one of the conditions for mediation (association of mediator with
the outcome under control of the predictor) is not satis�ed, we can conclude that there is no evidence for adverse events to mediate the

about the experimental diet. This phenomenon is called

The above phenomenon is best described as contamination of control participants. This can reduce the point estimate of the intervention's

questions.question_text:
A double-blind Randomised Controlled Trial is planned to study the e�ect of probiotic use in the treatment of anxiety. The researchers are
concerned that patients allocated to the placebo control group could also modify their diet and start taking supplemental probiotics if they
come to learn about the experimental diet. Which of the following methodological approach can reduce or avoid this e�ect?
questions.explanation:
Cluster randomisation allows entire groups of subjects that are geographically (or otherwise) clustered to be allocated to di�erent
treatments. This can potentially reduce the contact between control and active intervention arms and thus reduce treatment contamination.
Ref: Campbell MK, Grimshaw JM. Cluster randomised trials: time for improvement. BMJ. 1998;317:1171–1172.

questions.question_text:
A double-blind Randomised Controlled Trial is planned to study the e�ect of motivational counselling against alcohol use on the treatment
of depression in patients older than 35 years of age. The researchers recruit various General Practice surgeries for this purpose. The
intervention is allocated randomly to the General Practice surgeries, and once allocated, all patients recruited following their informed
consent at a centre are provided the same intervention (either counselling or place on a waiting-list). Which of the following bias is likely to
result from this approach?
questions.explanation:
This example describes a cluster-randomised trials where centres (not individuals) are randomised to treatment arms. This is called
clustering or trial-centre e�ect, de�ned as when observations are grouped together based upon common attributes. Such e�ect can also be
seen in multicentre trials where patients are clustered within centres, and trials where multiple therapists or surgeons are allocated to be
the providers of care. Clustering can lead to incorrect (i.e. too small) estimates of the precision and therefore incorrect type I error rates (i.e.
p values of the point estimate). Ref: Kahan BC, Morris TP. Assessing potential sources of clustering in individually randomised trials. BMC
medical research methodology. 2013 Dec;13(1):58.

questions.question_text: Which of the following can be used to reduce trial-centre e�ect in RCTs involving various general practice clusters?
questions.explanation:
Treatment assignments between patients in the same cluster will be correlated if patients in certain clusters are more likely to be in a certain
treatment group. This correlation is 1 in cluster RCTs wherein all patients recruited following their informed consent at a centre are provided
the same intervention. Simple randomisation where all patients are randomised independently leads to a zero-correlation among treatment
assignments. Ref: Kahan BC, Morris TP. Assessing potential sources of clustering in individually randomised trials. BMC medical research
methodology. 2013 Dec;13(1):58.

To investigate the 13-year risk of dementia and death in older adults with bipolar disorder, a cohort study of 37 768 men aged 65-85 years
was conducted. The outcomes dementia and death were traced from the data collected for The Health in Men Study (HIMS), a cohort study
of a community-representative sample of older Western Australian men that started in 1996. Follow-up data were censored on 30 June
2009, which is the last date for which data on cause-speci�c mortality are available. A total study sample of 37 768 older men who were alive
and free of dementia by 2 April 1996 were included in the investigation. Bipolar disorder was associated with increased adjusted hazard
ratio (HR) of dementia (HR = 2.30, 95% CI 1.80-2.94). Bipolar disorder was also associated with increased mortality (HR = 1.51, 95% CI 1.28-
1.77). See the graph below: With respect to the graph below, the rates of dementia appear to be very low at the beginning of the study. This
is due to
questions.explanation:
Right censoring occurs when a subject leaves the study before the event of interest (drop-out) or if the study ends before the event has
occurred. Right censoring is very common. Left censoring occurs if the event of interest (dementia) has already occurred before enrolment.
Right truncation occurs when the entire study population has already experienced the event of interest (i.e. dementia in this case). This can
be seen in historical surveys of patients who have the outcome of interest from a registry (e.g. the use of a dementia registry for this
question). Left truncation occurs when the subjects have been at risk before entering the study. In this study, left truncation is negligible as
the risk of dementia is smaller before the age of 65. Ref: www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~mlunn/lecturenotes1.pdf

questions.question_text:
Concord grape juice is said to improve memory. To investigate this further, 230 ml purple grape juice or sugar-matched control was
administered to 20 elderly subjects living in Newcastle-upon-Tyne and surrounding areas. The subjects received both interventions in a
double-blind manner after 6-7 days of washout period in a random sequence. Computerised measures of episodic memory, working
memory, attention and mood were completed at baseline and following a 20-min absorption period. Purple grape juice signi�cantly
improved reaction time on a composite attention measure (p = 0.047) and increased calm ratings (p = 0.046) when compared to placebo.
Order e�ects also indicated an enduring positive e�ect on pre-dose memory reaction time (p = 0.018) and post-dose calm ratings (p = 0.019)
when purple grape was consumed �rst. No signi�cant e�ects of juice were observed on memory measures. Which of the following best
describes the above study design?
questions.explanation: This is a randomised, placebo-controlled, double blind crossover study.

administered to 20 elderly subjects living in Newcastle-upon-Tyne and surrounding areas. The subjects received both interventions in a
double-blind manner after 6-7 days of washout period in a random sequence. Computerised measures of episodic memory, working
memory, attention and mood were completed at baseline and following a 20-min absorption period. Purple grape juice signi�cantly
improved reaction time on a composite attention measure (p = 0.047) and increased calm ratings (p = 0.046) when compared to placebo.
Order e�ects also indicated an enduring positive e�ect on pre-dose memory reaction time (p = 0.018) and post-dose calm ratings (p = 0.019)
when purple grape was consumed �rst. No signi�cant e�ects of juice were observed on memory measures. Which of the following limitation
is partially mitigated by the crossover design?
questions.explanation:
A crossover design has several advantages over a parallel RCT. As the subjects in both arms are essentially the same, the comparability of
study and control groups with regard to confounding variables (e.g., age and sex) is greatly enhanced. Ina ddition, trials with a crossover
design require lower sample sizes than parallel-group trials to meet the same criteria in terms of type I and type II error risks.

questions.question_text:
To assess whether maternal use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) increases the risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension in
the newborn, a population based cohort study using data from the national health registers from Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and
Sweden, between 1996-2007. Comparisons were made between infants exposed and not exposed to SSRIs. Around 30 000 women had used
SSRIs during pregnancy and 11 014 had been dispensed an SSRI later than gestational week 20. Exposure to SSRIs in late pregnancy was
associated with an increased risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension in the newborn: 33 of 11 014 exposed infants (absolute risk 3 per
1000 liveborn infants compared with the background incidence of 1.2 per 1000); adjusted odds ratio 2.1 (95% con�dence interval 1.5 to 3.0).
The increased risks of persistent pulmonary hypertension in the newborn for each of the speci�c SSRIs (sertraline, citalopram, paroxetine,
and �uoxetine) were of similar magnitude. Filling a prescription with SSRIs before gestational week 8 yielded slightly increased risks:
adjusted odds ratio 1.4 (95% con�dence interval 1.0 to 2.0). Ref: Kieler H, et al. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors during pregnancy and
risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension in the newborn: population based cohort study from the �ve Nordic countries. BMJ. 2012 Jan
12;344:d8012. Which of the following is a valid conclusion from this study?

options.text: The use of SSRIs in early pregnancy increases the risk of PPHN
The use of SSRIs in late pregnancy reduces the risk of PPHN
The use of SSRIs in pregnancy is not advisable
The use of SSRIs in late pregnancy increases the risk of PPHN
The use of SSRIs in early pregnancy reduces the risk of PPHN

correct_answer.text: The use of SSRIs in late pregnancy increases the risk of PPHN

questions.explanation:
The results suggest that the absolute risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn is low (1.2 per 1000), but use of SSRIs in late
pregnancy increases that risk more than twofold (by a factor of 2.1). The increased risk appears to be a class e�ect, a�ecting all SSRIs. In
early pregnancy the increased risk is not statistically signi�cant.

There is a potential association between Paroxetine in late pregnancy and PPHN

questions.explanation:
We cannot directly infer the risk of other non-SSRI antidepressants from the data presented to us. So statement A is incorrect. We cannot

questions.question_text:
Harwood et al. analysed the data from California Drug and Alcohol Treatment Assessment of 1992 to investigate the economic bene�ts of
methadone use in women and men (Table from Cartwright WS. Cost–bene�t analysis of drug treatment services: review of the literature.
The Journal of Mental Health Policy and Economics. 2000 Mar;3(1):11-26.). Women were 38% of the total treatment population and averaged
$1381 per patient in treatment cost. From the information presented, which of the following is a valid conclusion that can be derived? Using
methadone for detoxi�cation is:

options.text: Good value for both men and women
Good value for men but not for women
Good value for women but not for men
No comment can be made on the value of methadone

correct_answer.text: Good value for men but not for women

questions.explanation:
CBA or cost-bene�t analysis is an economic evaluation of the costs of an intervention compared to the bene�ts of the intervention, with
both costs and bene�ts measured in the same monetary units. Comparing the economic expenditure imposed by participants before
treatment with the expenditures incurred due to and after the treatment helps us to assess the ‘bene�ts' of a treatment. Costs that are
avoided (by intervening) results in bene�ts. Bene�ts take on a negative value if economic costs are greater during or after treatment

questions.question_text:
Expectations and preconceptions can potentially taint the process of qualitative research. Which of the following methods is used in
qualitative research to mitigate the potentially deleterious e�ects of researcher preconceptions?
questions.explanation:
Bracketing includes a set of methods that stem from a researcher's commitment to surfacing his or her preconceptions both before and
during the qualitative research process. The various bracketing approaches include methods such as (1) keeping a re�exive journal begun
prior to de�ning the research question (2) engaging in interviews with an outside source to uncover and bring into awareness
preconceptions and biases (3) writing memos throughout data collection and analysis as a means of examining and re�ecting upon the
researcher's engagement with the data. Ref: Excerpts from Tu�ord L, Newman P. Bracketing in qualitative research. Qualitative social work.
2012 Jan;11(1):80-96.

questions.question_text:
Stalking is a relatively common phenomenon and often leads to the victims experiencing signi�cant distress due to disruption to their life
and fear of being physically harmed. Which of the following types of stalker poses the greatest risk of sexual violence?
questions.explanation:
In a landmark study of stalker conducted by Mullen et al (1999), 5 types of stalkers were recognized: rejected, intimacy seeking, incompetent,
resentful, and predatory. Delusional disorders were common (30%), particularly among intimacy-seeking stalkers, while personality
disorders predominated among rejected stalkers. The duration of stalking was longer for rejected and intimacy-seeking stalkers. 63% of the
stalkers (N=84) made threats, and 36% (N=52) were assaultive. Threats and property damage were more frequent with resentful stalkers,
but rejected and predatory stalkers committed more assaults. Committing assault was also predicted by previous convictions, substance-
related disorders, and previous threats. Predatory stalkers were the smallest group (<3%), but predominantly had paraphilias and were
more likely than all other groups to have previous convictions for sexual o�enses and were highly likely to commit sexual assaults on the
stalked victims. Ref: Excerpt adapted from Mullen PE, Purcell R, Stuart GW. Study of stalkers. American journal of psychiatry. 1999 Aug
1;156(8):1244-9.

questions.question_text:
Homicide-suicide is a rare but serious event when an individual will kill another person, usually current or past partners, before ending their
own life. Which of the following mental disorders is most associated with this event?
questions.explanation:
The most common mental health diagnosis associated with homicide-suicide in intimate or family relations, is depression. Other diagnoses
are rare. Case series report that the typical homicide-suicide case involves a depressed, controlling husband who shoots his ill wife. Ref;
Rosenbaum M. The role of depression in couples involved in murder-suicide and homicide. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 1990 Aug
1;147(8):1036.

Autism spectrum disorders are not generally associated with a marked increase in the commission of criminal acts. Which of the following is

Based on sentencing statistics, �re-setting may be the most common crime carried out by people with ASD (Dein & Woodbury-Smith, 2010).

reo�ending?

options.text: Having exposed himself to people of di�erent ages

questions.explanation:
Earlier onset of o�ending is associated with recidivism. Many exhibitionists have prior criminal histories and around 30% will go on to
commit other sexual o�ences. Victimizing individuals of various ages is associated with an increased risk of reo�ending. Alcohol misuse and

questions.question_text:
Miss Olive Charleston is a 32-year-old woman with moderate intellectual disability and has been su�ering from otitis externa for the past 10
days. The sta� members in her care home have observed her banging her head on doors and tables. They attributed this behaviour to her
intellectual disability and have been trying to reassure and distract her without success. Which of the following best describes this
phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Diagnostic overshadowing is the attribution of a person's symptoms to their mental condition, when such symptoms actually suggest a
comorbid condition. The term was �rst used to describe the under-diagnosis of mental illness in people with intellectual disability. In recent
years, the term has also been used when physical illnesses are overlooked in people with mental illness. Ref: Mason J, Scior K. ‘Diagnostic
overshadowing' amongst clinicians working with people with intellectual disabilities in the UK. Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual
Disabilities. 2004 Jun;17(2):85-90.

questions.question_text:
Miss Amber O'Neill is a 48-year-old woman with a history of mild intellectual disability who usually lives in a supported accommodation. She
has presented to the GP with a history of intermittent rectal bleeding over the past two weeks. She has refused a PR examination as she
worries it will be painful and embarrassing although she permitted an abdominal exam. Her physical observations are normal and she
appears to be clinically stable. Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Check previous case notes to determine if she has capacity to refuse the examination
Give her a sedative so you can perform the examination
Ask the practice nurse to hold her while you perform the examination
Delay the examination and explain the procedure in simpler terms to the patient

correct_answer.text: Delay the examination and explain the procedure in simpler terms to the patient

questions.explanation:
It would be most appropriate to try and enhance the patient's capacity by taking the additional time to explain the examination in an
appropriate way and with suitable language. This may enable the patient to understand the rationale for the investigation and possibly
consent. Her capacity in this situation cannot be determined from previous notes and it would not be acceptable to compel her to have the
examination.

questions.question_text:
Miss Jane Williams is a 34-year-old woman with a diagnosis of Down's syndrome and moderate intellectual disability. She lives with her
mother who is struggling with her physical health. Her mother is aware that Miss Williams is at an increased risk of developing Alzheimer's
disease and is wondering about what she might see if this occurs. Which of the following is a more common presentation for Alzheimer's
disease in people with Down's syndrome compared to those without?
questions.explanation:
Personality change manifesting in the form of behavioural and psychological symptoms appear to be a common presenting feature of
Alzheimer's disease in individuals with Down's syndrome compared to the general population. This is even more frequent amongst younger
individuals and those with more severe intellectual impairments. These prominent personality and behaviour changes, associated with
executive dysfunction, may indicate a frontal involvement, but the pathological diagnosis is likely to be Alzheimer's in most cases. Ref: Ball
SL, et al. Personality and behaviour changes mark the early stages of Alzheimer's disease in adults with Down's syndrome: �ndings from a
prospective population-based study. International Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry. 2006 Jul;21(7):661-73.

questions.question_text:
Mr Mark Phillips is a 27-year-old man with a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder and mild intellectual disability. He is currently living in a
residential placement with 24-hour carers available. They have noted that he does not sleep regularly at night and this impairs his
functioning during the day. They have tried to address this via non-pharmacological methods but have not been successful. Which of the
following would be the most appropriate management plan for him?
questions.explanation:
Sleep disturbance is relatively common in people with autism spectrum disorders. This is thought to be due to an abnormality in circadian
rhythm and is best treated with melatonin. Ref: Andersen IM et al. Melatonin for insomnia in children with autism spectrum disorders.
Journal of child neurology. 2008 May;23(5):482-5.

questions.question_text:
Ian Moss is a 7-year-old boy who has been found to have mild intellectual impairment following an assessment carried out by the
community paediatric team. He is also noted to have a long face, large ears and macro-orchidism. Which of the following syndromes does
he most likely su�er from?
questions.explanation:
This description is characteristic of Fragile X. This is more severe in males and is inherited in a X-linked dominant fashion. Individuals with
this disorder can also have ASD traits and ADHD symptoms, as well as di�culties with anxiety. Around 10% will experience seizures.

questions.question_text:
Patients with intellectual impairment can develop co-morbid psychotic illnesses. There is often a signi�cant delay in diagnosis in these
individuals. Which of the following is most likely to account for this?

options.text: Patients often not in contact with health or statutory services
Little change can be seen in their behaviour

questions.explanation:
The primary di�culty in diagnosing psychotic illness, as well as other co-morbid physical and mental illnesses, in those with intellectual
impairment is communication. Individuals may not have language for their experiences or very limited ability to communicate verbally or
non-verbally. They may show signi�cant change in behaviour but interpreting this can be challenging. Ref: Welch KA, et al. Systematic Review
of the Clinical Presentation of Schizophrenia in Intellectual Disability. J Psychopathol Behav Assess2011;33:246

questions.question_text:
Kyle Reece is a 6-year-old boy who has moderate intellectual impairment and microcephaly. He shows marked self-injurious behaviour,
which has led to him requiring signi�cant medical care. Which of the following syndromes is he most likely to have?
questions.explanation:
Lesch–Nyhan syndrome or Juvenile Gout is caused by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) de�ciency due to X-
chromosomal mutation in the HPRT gene. So it is exclusively a male disorder. Patients su�er from manifestations of high levels of uric acid
production. This results in both hyperuricemia and hyperuricosuria, leading to severe gout and often, renal complications. Many a�ected
children have moderate intellectual disability, along with abnormal involuntary muscle movements including dystonia, chorea and in some
cases, ballismus. In addition to requiring wheelchairs for mobility, many will need assistance to sit. Beginning in the second year of life, a
particularly striking feature of LNS is self-mutilating behaviors, characterized by lip and �nger biting. It is also associated with microcephaly.

questions.question_text: Deletions of speci�c genes can lead to characteristic phenotypes. Which of the following disorders is the result of a gene deletion?
questions.explanation:
Turner Syndrome is caused by the loss of an entire X chromosome, leading to a XO genotype. Fragile X, tuberous sclerosis and Lesch Nyhan
syndromes are due to gene mutations, while Prader Willi is due to uniparental disomy or genomic imprinting.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Tanya Walters is a 75-year-old woman with an existing diagnosis of mild Alzheimer's dementia. Over the past 5 weeks her family have
noticed that she has been persistent low in mood, withdrawn and has shown no interest in activities, which she used to enjoy. On
assessment, she expresses feeling “useless” and constantly tired. Which of the following would be the most appropriate management plan
at this point?

options.text: Urine dip and blood tests to exclude organic causes

correct_answer.text: Urine dip and blood tests to exclude organic causes

questions.explanation:
While patients with dementia can become depressed and require antidepressant medication or other interventions, they are more
vulnerable than the general population to developing mood disturbance in response to organic illness, which may not be immediately
apparent. It is prudent to check for organic illness before o�ering an antidepressant. Remember that MDD is a disorder of exclusion in the
elderly. SSRIs are more appropriate than tricyclics in the older population who may have cardiac disease or be on other medications with
potential drug interactions.

questions.question_text:
Mr Benjamin Wyles is a 77-year-old man with a history of recurrent depressive disorder. He is currently experiencing a severe episode of
depression and his appetite is very poor. His illness has not responded to 3 adequate trials of antidepressants. Which of the following is the
most appropriate treatment for him at this stage?
questions.explanation:
The patient is experiencing a severe treatment resistant episode of depression with marked appetite disturbance. It would be reasonable to
treat him with ECT to achieve rapid improvement and address his appetite disturbance while also continuing antidepressants. Older patients
can receive ECT and often respond well.

questions.question_text:
Older people who express suicidal ideation or attempt suicide are at greater future risk than younger patients. Which of the following is
most associated with suicide in old age?
questions.explanation:
Avoidant and anankastic personality disorder are associated with increased risk of suicide in older people. Histrionic personality disorder is
associated with a lower risk of suicide. All personality disorders are associated with an increased risk of suicidal ideation. Male gender, being
widowed and having a lower openness to experience are associated with an increased risk of suicide in older age.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Lisbeth Slander is a 79-year-old woman who has progressively developed loss of memory, visual hallucinations and intermittent
irritability over the course of several months. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for her condition?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to represent Lewy Body Dementia, which is characterized by memory impairment, perceptual disturbances and mood
changes. The �rst line of treatment is acetyl cholinesterase inhibitors, such as Rivastigamine.

questions.question_text:
Mr Yann deWael is a 70-year-old man with a diagnosis of refractory depression. He is currently experiencing a severe depressive episode,
which is not responding to antidepressant treatment. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for him?
questions.explanation:
ECT has the best evidence for e�ectiveness in treatment resistant depression and can be used in the acute phase and as maintenance.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation is increasingly being used in clinical practice. Vague nerve stimulation is an uncommon treatment that can
be used after other options have been exhausted. Stimulants have been used in treatment resistant depression but the evidence for them is
limited. A meta-analysis has suggested that ECT is superior to high frequency rTMS in terms of response and remission while discontinuation
was not signi�cantly di�erent between the two treatments. There was insu�cient data on medium or long-term e�cacy. Results based on 3
studies suggested that speci�c cognitive domains such as visual memory and verbal �uency were more impaired in patients receiving ECT
than TMS. This review highlighted a lack of good quality trials comparing the long-term outcome and cognitive e�ects of rTMS and ECT,
especially using approaches to optimize stimulus delivery and reduce clinical heterogeneity. Ref: Ren J, Li H, Palaniyappan L, et al. Repetitive
transcranial magnetic stimulation versus electroconvulsive therapy for major depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Progress in
Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry. 2014 Jun 3;51:181-9.

questions.question_text:
Atypical antipsychotics are known to increase the risk of cerebrovascular complications when taken by older people. What is the factor by
which atypical antipsychotics increase the risk of stroke in older people?
questions.explanation:
Older people receiving atypical antipsychotics are 2.3 times more likely to experience a stroke than those who are unexposed. This increases
to 5.9 times if the individual has a diagnosis of dementia. The respective risks for typical antipsychotics are 1.7 and 3.3 times respectively. In
patients with dementia, exposure to any antipsychotic increased rate of stroke by 3.5 times and by 1.4 times in people without dementia.
Ref: Douglas IJ, Smeeth L. Exposure to antipsychotics and risk of stroke: self-controlled case series study.BMJ 2008; 337:a1227

questions.question_text:
Huntington's disease is a degenerative neurological condition that usually arises in middle life and leads to movement disorders, cognitive
impairment, a�ective symptoms and sometimes features of psychosis. Which of the following is most appropriate for con�rming its
diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Gene testing is usually conducted to con�rm the diagnosis of Huntington's. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and is due to a
triple repeat expansion in chromosome 4p.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Abigail Baker is a 78-year-old woman with a diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia who experiences marked insomnia, which she �nds
distressing during the night. She also has di�culties with recurrent falls and there are concerns that these will occur if she wanders during
the night. Which of the following would be the most appropriate pharmacological intervention for her?
questions.explanation:
Melatonin would be most appropriate as it is not directly sedating and acts via melatonin receptors and the circadian rhythm. Any sedating
agent increases the risk of falls.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Amal Khan is a 73-year-old woman with a diagnosis of a severe depressive episode, which has not been responsive to 3 trials of
antidepressant medication. Electroconvulsive therapy is now being considered and her family want to know if there are any circumstances
under which this should absolutely not be used. Which of the following is a relative contraindication for ECT?
questions.explanation:
The sole absolute contraindication for ECT is a known phaeochromocytoma. Increased intracranial pressure, current intracranial masses,
recent stroke, cardiac conduction abnormalities, high risk pregnancy, aortic and cerebral aneurysms, asthma/COPD treated with
theophylline are relative contraindications. Unstable angina, decompensated heart failure, severe valvular disease, uncontrolled diabetes
and severe gastro-oesophageal re�ux may require special consideration.

questions.question_text: With regard to supporting caregivers of patients with dementia, which of the following is the best evidence based recommendation?

options.text: Interventions o�ered from distance are not e�ective
Shorter and simple interventions are not e�ective for most carers
Supplying written information is the intervention most supported by current evidence
A multicomponent approach across di�erent times is recommended
All carers must be referred to local Alzheimer's Society groups

correct_answer.text: A multicomponent approach across di�erent times is recommended

questions.explanation:
The evidence base for psychosocial interventions to support carers of patients with dementia is expanding, but still �rm conclusions cannot
be reached due to lack of well replicated, homogenous studies. According to a recent review (Jackson & Browne, 2017), “support
interventions are more likely to be e�ective if: (1) multiple supports are o�ered (i.e. a multicomponent approach is taken) (2) educational
interventions are designed to provide opportunity for active learning (e.g. role-play scenarios rather than ‘information only') (3) the more
complicated an intervention is, the less likely a carer is to adhere to it (4) distance interventions can be e�ective and should be considered,
especially for older carers and those in isolated rural locations (5) Simply allocating a speci�c keyworker, supplying written only information
or referring on to peer support groups are not likely to be e�ective”. Ref: Excerpts from Jackson GA, Browne D. Supporting carers of people
with dementia: what is e�ective?. BJPsych Advances. 2017 May;23(3):179-86.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is most likely to be correct with regard to nondegenerative dementias?

options.text: They cannot be reversed with treatment
Depression is not a common feature
Multiple sclerosis is a known risk factor
Agnosia, aphasia, and apraxia are often seen early in the course.
Patients usually present with features of a cortical dementia.

correct_answer.text: Multiple sclerosis is a known risk factor

questions.explanation:
Cognitive impairment is often seen in MS and is the leading predictor of occupational disability, but unlike Alzheimer's, fronto-temporal or
Lewy Body Dementia, MS related cognitive impairment is considered to be non degenerative.

questions.question_text:
You are delivering psychotherapy to a patient who has been experiencing low mood and feelings of inadequacy. You have noticed that when
you return home you tend to feel anxious and like you are not a good enough therapist. Which of the following best describes what is
happening?
questions.explanation:
This is likely to describe projective identi�cation with the patient projecting his or her own feelings into another individual, in this case the
therapist. This is distinct from countertransference, where the patient evokes feelings in the therapist that are around the patient
themselves.

questions.question_text:
A defence mechanism is an unconscious psychological mechanism that reduces anxiety arising from unacceptable or potentially harmful
stimuli. They can be psychotic/pathological, immature, neurotic or mature. Which of the following is a neurotic defence mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Neurotic defenses include: displacement, dissociation, intellectualisation, reaction formation, repression, isolation, rationalisation,
regression, undoing, withdrawal and social comparisons.

questions.question_text:
Family therapy is often used in situations where it is thought that interactions within the family structure are contributing to the illness that
the individual is experiencing. There are various models of family therapy and similar interventions. Which of the following uses 'reframing
and evaluation of roles’ in the family?
questions.explanation:
Structural family therapy uses techniques such as reframing and evaluation of roles within the family. The therapist aims to "enter" into the
family to understand the roles and how these are causing di�culties. They aim to disrupt and modify how family members interact and the
roles they hold within the family system.

questions.question_text:
Guided self-help can be useful intervention is some conditions. It works by assisting the individual to understand their di�culties and then
make positive changes, usually in keeping with an established treatment protocol. Which of the following is it most likely to be helpful for?
questions.explanation:
NICE recommends guided self-help in depression and anxiety disorders. It can be used in bulimia nervosa but the evidence base is not as
strong.

questions.question_text:
Some psychotherapeutic interventions use hypothesising as part of their process to alleviate patient symptoms. Which of the following uses
'hypothesising’?
questions.explanation:
A therapist hypothesising regarding a patient's current experiences and symptoms and how these may relate to past experiences or
patterns is a central element of psychodynamic psychotherapy. This term is also used often by Milan school of systemic family therapists,
but in a slightly di�erent context. In systemic family therapy, hypothesising is "the formulation of systemic 'suppositions' that guaranteed
therapist activity, gave order to the interview and oriented the questioning. Hypotheses are based on positive connotation, attempted to
make sense of the problem in the relational context, but did not seek to access the truth. The three systemic principles of hypothesising,
circularity and neutrality are primarily employed by systemic family therapists as methods for interviewing families. These approaches also
reduce the emphasis on the therapist personal qualities such as intuition, charisma and concern that can occur in a therapy setting". Ref:
Excerpts from Brown JM. The Milan principles of hypothesising, circularity and neutrality in dialogical family therapy: Extinction, evolution,
eviction... or emergence?. Australian and New Zealand Journal of Family Therapy. 2010 Sep;31(3):248-65.

questions.question_text:
Mr Jeremy Blunt is a 41-year-old health executive, who is currently undergoing psychodynamic psychotherapy. During a regular session, he
informs the therapist that he recently went to see a Reiki practitioner and feels that it is a "wonderful cure" and "holds the answer to all his
di�culties". Which of the following would best describe this phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
This would match best with idealization whereby an individual has an uncritically positive view of another person or object. This occurs in
splitting, but with denigration, or an absolutely negative view, of another person or object. However, this is absent in this example.

questions.question_text:
Yalom described various factors which he theorised were important to the outcome of therapy in a group setting. Which of the following
describes Yalom’s existential factor?

options.text: Taking on positive aspects of others
Being aware of emotions of the whole group
Understanding the futility of attempting to change the actions of others
Understanding that one’s experiences are similar to those of others
Learning to exist as part of something larger than oneself

correct_answer.text: Learning to exist as part of something larger than oneself

questions.explanation:
Yalom described eleven therapeutic factors that in�uence change and healing in group therapy. One among them is an existential factor. It
incorporates learning how to exist just as a part of something larger than oneself. This factor brings a client into the awareness that life will
continue on, with pain, death, sadness, regret, and joy. By living existentially, clients learn how to accept these conditions without escaping
from them. Instead, they learn how to live with them and through them.

questions.question_text:
Family therapy is often used in situations where it is thought that interactions within the family structure are contributing to the illness that
the individual is experiencing. There are various models of family therapy and similar interventions. Which of the following uses 'homework
assignments’ for the family?
questions.explanation:
Strategic family therapy is most associated with use of homework for families. This is often used to disrupt family patterns paradoxically, e.g.
telling a child who tends to have tantrums to have them more often.

questions.question_text:
Cognitive analytic therapy is structured into established steps, which the patient moves through over the course of the sessions. Which of
the following occurs in the initial sessions of CAT?
questions.explanation:
The initial sessions of CAT are devoted to gathering information about current di�culties and previous experiences, after which the
therapist writes the patient a reformulation letter. This phase is followed by a recognition phase where the patient is helped via various
means to acknowledge their di�culties and how they occur. This is followed by a revision phase where the patient and therapist plan
together how the patient will cease unhelpful behaviours and patterns of thinking.

questions.question_text:
A new Machine Learning Algorithm (MLA) is compared to the validated NAPLS-2 criteria for predicting conversion to psychosis in subjects
that are identi�ed to have a Clinical High Risk (CHR) status. 24 of 400 CHR subjects are predicted to convert in the next 2 years, according to
the NAPLS-2 criteria. The MLA identi�es 40 of the 400 as potential converters to psychosis, with 16 subjects being identi�ed as converters by
both the NAPLS-2 criteria and the MLA. What is the sensitivity of the MLA in predicting conversion to psychosis from the CHR state?
questions.explanation:
To answer this question, �rst construct a 2X2 table. The values provided in the question can be used to �ll the cells as below. Sensitivity =
true positive (16) divided by total 'diseased' (24) = 16/24 = 2/3 = 67%
